For 637 Atlantic and eastern North Pacific tropical cyclones from the 2002-2023 hurricane seasons, we analyze the discussion text and its combination with 13 hurricane environmental predictors from SHIPS and ERA5 10-meter wind fields, for forecasting intensity changes at lead times of 24 to 120 hours using three modeling methods. In one approach, an end-to-end deep learning framework for the text shows that the discussions alone offer comparable value for 24-hour intensity forecasts to the SHIPS predictors. Adding discussion information to the SHIPS predictors in an ensemble of five such models reduces the mean absolute error of 24-hour maximum sustained wind forecasts for 2022-2023 cyclones from 9.89 to 8.90 kt, with a confidence interval that excludes zero when whole storms are resampled. The ERA5 wind fields have a minor effect on mean absolute error in wind predictions, and model rankings differ across predicted variables, lead times and model types. We provide prediction intervals for these forecasts, whose coverage falls below the 90% target during rapid intensification. Analysis of the text shows that words related to intensity and intensity change (such as intensify, weaken, eyewall and category) are important for the model predictions. This retrospective study shows the added value of the forecasters' discussions and suggests that multi-modal learning can help understand the predictive contribution of expert human judgment. The reanalysis data differ from real-time analyses, and the discussions are issued at least three hours after the valid time of the other inputs, so these results should not be interpreted operationally.

title: How VLMs Plan What's Next
summary: When a vision-language model describes an image, it names one object at a time and it rarely repeats itself, yet how the model plans this order is far from obvious. We characterize the mechanism a VLM uses to decide where to look before it looks. The mechanism has four main parts. First, binding heads match the relevant text tokens against the image and resolve them into pointers to the matched image region. Second, the same binding heads bind each written answer to the region it came from, and the model turns it into a progress signal: a cursor, the position in the image up to which the list has been written. Third, a select step chooses the nearest unwritten region after the cursor, or stops. Finally, gaze heads execute the chosen pointer and return a concept of what is drawn there, which language heads and the late MLPs turn into a word in the language of the question. We validate each part of this mechanism through causal patching in Qwen3-VL models on a synthetic visual retrieval task, and test our mechanisms against alternative hypotheses. We further show that the mechanism holds across input formats, natural photographs, and languages, and that its binding, relay, and gaze heads appear at every model size from 2B to 32B. This work allows us to investigate how a VLM turns a question and an image into a sequence of answers, layer by layer and token by token. More broadly, it opens a way to study how models plan over complex multi-step tasks with long rollouts. Our project is available at https://plan.baulab.info/

title: Hyperlyve: Parallelized Enumeration and Exact Lyapunov Stability Certification for Deep ReLU Networks
summary: We introduce Hyperlyve (Hyperplane Partitioned Lyapunov Verification and Enumeration), a framework for proving the asymptotic stability of nonlinear dynamical systems, including those with neural network controllers. Hyperlyve learns and formally certifies continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) neural Lyapunov functions within a counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS) loop. Hyperlyve's key innovation is a parallel algorithm that enumerates the hyperplane arrangement formed by the ReLU activations of deep networks and certifies that Lyapunov conditions hold within each polyhedral region. We derive sound and complete regional tests to verify the asymptotic stability of the exact smooth dynamics (rather than a piecewise-linear approximation) within a compact domain of interest. Furthermore, we formally characterize the computational complexity of the CPA neural Lyapunov verification problem as co-NP-complete, filling a key gap in the literature. Empirical results demonstrate that Hyperlyve enumerates ReLU networks over 150-times faster than competing tools, which contributes to Hyperlyve proving the asymptotic stability of systems that are currently intractable for state-of-the-art verifiers.

title: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting with Physics-Indexed Specialist Memory: the Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent
summary: Continual reinforcement learning requires adaptation to changing conditions while preserving performance under previously encountered dynamics. It was investigated whether specialists generated by evolutionary search can provide a reusable memory when combined with environment detection and failure-driven search. The Evolutionary Neuroplastic Agent (ENA) evolves small neural networks without gradients, archives selected policies by detected dynamic regime, and retrieves them through Bayesian policy reuse. The architecture was evaluated in non-stationary CartPole and HalfCheetah environments. In the 30-replicate CartPole ablation, the complete architecture achieved a mean success rate of 83.2% across the five test environments. Among variants that learned the harder CartPole environments, the complete architecture showed the most consistent retention. A selection ablation also showed that the retrieval rule affected performance. In the evaluated sequences, ENA adapted more slowly than PPO on CartPole and achieved lower returns than SAC on HalfCheetah. The evidence concerns the complete architecture and does not isolate gradient-free optimization as the cause of retention or establish superiority over other continual-learning methods.

title: Optimal Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought Learning via Bagging
summary: We study how to learn an autoregressive next-token generator $f\colonΣ^\star\toΣ$ from a class $\mathcal{F}$, given chain-of-thought (CoT) demonstrations of length $T$ generated by $f$. We present a simple algorithm based on bagging, which outputs a majority vote of generators that are trained to be CoT-consistent on bootstrap samples of the training data. For binary token sets, it achieves the optimal sample complexity of $O((d_{\mathrm{VC}}+\log(1/δ))/ε)$, independent of the CoT length $T$, where $d_{\mathrm{VC}}$ is the VC dimension of $\mathcal{F}$. For finite token sets $Σ$, the VC dimension is replaced by a multiclass analogue, the Graph dimension $d_{\mathrm{G}}$, and the sample complexity is optimal up to a $\log|Σ|$ factor. The number of generators in the majority-vote ensemble is $O(\log(T/δ))$, and we show that the ensemble can be distilled into a single generator in $\mathcal{F}$ at the expense of $n\log(nT)$ unlabeled prompts.

title: SADL: On the Demand-Supply Geometry of Representation Collapse
summary: In Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), a well-constrained projector output does not by itself prevent representation collapse. We find that, from initialization, the encoder representation is dominated by a component shared by different inputs. A batch-normalized projector removes this component, so regularization after the projector cannot correct it, and the differences between representations shrink until they collapse. We propose SADL (Supply And Demand Loss), which keeps the original training objective and constrains the encoder directly when needed. SADL compares the representation differences that the projector output demands with the differences the encoder can retain and pass on to the projector, and adds a constraint on the encoder only when supply falls short of demand. It works with different Demand Regularizers and introduces no auxiliary networks, additional trainable parameters, or architectural changes. In single-task and jointly trained four-task LeWorldModel (LeWM) and INTACT experiments, SADL lowers the collapse rate over ten random seeds from 50% to 0%. After one epoch of training, encoder effective rank is 3.4-6.4 times that of the corresponding baseline without SADL, and latent prediction error falls to 1/20-1/303 of it. Without additional tuning, SADL stays robust as its loss weight spans orders of magnitude, and with several Demand Regularizers INTACT exceeds 95% mean search-free control success. On four image datasets, SADL also consistently improves accuracy and stability across random seeds. These results show that matching the representation differences a regularizer demands with the differences the encoder can supply leads to faster and more stable representation learning in control and image classification.

title: Surrogate-Assisted Compact-Model Extraction for SKY130 CMOS at 77 K
summary: Cryogenic circuit design requires compact transistor models that reproduce measured low-temperature behavior and run in standard circuit simulators. We fit BSIM4 parameters to measured I-V curves of SkyWater 130 nm (SKY130) transistors at 77 K using a neural surrogate of NGSpice. The surrogate maps compact-model parameters and device geometry to the complete set of output and transfer characteristics. Extraction is a bounded least-squares search: a bank of NGSpice simulations supplies initial candidates, finite differences of the surrogate supply the local Jacobian, and NGSpice re-simulates the resulting cards before selection. On 18 measured geometries, we compare a search over seven card parameters with a search over 43 parameters selected by NGSpice sensitivity. Relative to NGSpice re-simulations of the previously released cards, the two searches reduce the in-sample mean relative root-mean-square error (RRMS) by 17% and 26%, respectively. The 43-parameter search has the lower overall error, but the seven-parameter search has the lower mean on high-bias curves, and some individual curves have higher error than with the released cards under both searches.

title: CertiSum: Bitwise-Identical MXFP4 Training Across Platforms and Parallelism Layouts
summary: Training with MXFP4, a 4-bit microscaling format, is non-deterministic: identical inputs can produce different results across parallelism layouts and GPU vendors. These differences complicate debugging and training audits and can cause training and inference engines to disagree. We present CertiSum to make MXFP4 training bitwise invariant across runs, parallelism layouts, and GPU vendors. Its key insight is that native FP32 accumulation of MXFP4 products is often already exact for every summation order. CertiSum collects statistics during quantization to certify native matrix multiplication results, recomputes uncertified outputs exactly, and uses exact kernels directly where certification rarely succeeds. CertiSum keeps quantization blocks unchanged across layouts and merges partial sums without rounding, including in attention and weight-gradient computation. In 200-step Qwen3-8B-Base experiments, CertiSum preserves training states bit for bit across AMD MI350X and NVIDIA GB200 and across changes in data, tensor, and context parallelism on MI350X. Across three 8B--14B models on FineWeb-Edu using MI350X, it adds 11.8--60.5% to training-step latency relative to its non-exact MXFP4 counterpart at the larger evaluated input shapes, with speedups of up to $1.24\times$ over BF16 and $1.70\times$ over deterministic BF16.

title: DynSurvX: Time-Resolved Explanations for Dynamic Survival Predictions
summary: Recent survival models integrating longitudinal data achieve strong predictive performance, but their predictions are often difficult to interpret, limiting their clinical use. We propose DynSurvX, a model-agnostic explainability framework for dynamic survival prediction with mixed static and longitudinal covariates. Based on Shapley values, DynSurvX introduces a hierarchical two-phase strategy that first identifies influential longitudinal features and then adaptively refines their temporal importance, enabling fine-grained explanations while reducing computational cost. The framework provides time-resolved explanations that evolve as new patient data become available. Experiments on simulated and two clinical datasets show varying agreement with theoretical importance across prediction models, with closer agreement for better-performing models, alongside clinically interpretable insights in real-world settings. It remains robust across prediction settings and reduces computation time by 41--80\% relative to the temporal explanation baseline, making dynamic explanations practical.

title: When Do Histology Foundation Models Need Geometric Test-Time Augmentation?
summary: Test-time augmentation (TTA) aggregates model predictions across multiple transformed views of an input during inference. Because histology images lack a canonical orientation, $D_4$ TTA---pooling across the 8 rotations and reflections of a square---is a standard default in computational pathology. However, the rise of self-supervised histology foundation models (FMs) with inherent rotational invariance calls its continued utility into question. We benchmark 9 histology FMs and 6 general-purpose models across four patch-level and two whole-slide image (WSI) datasets. We find that $D_4$ TTA remains a reliable post hoc improvement, but benefits diminish from $+1.98$ percentage points (pp) for general-purpose backbones to $+0.50$ pp for histology FMs on TCGA-UT, and shrink further for the largest models. To eliminate computational overhead, our experiments demonstrate that entropy routing---applying TTA selectively to uncertain predictions---recovers most of the gain while augmenting only ${\sim}13\%$ of samples. Finally, we show that patch-level TTA improvements do not transfer to slide-level multiple instance learning (MIL). Code: https://github.com/lars-chen/histology-tta

title: Severe but Harmless: Stress-Testing Shift Severity for Frozen Time-Series Forecasters
summary: Zero-shot time-series foundation models (TSFMs) have become attractive alternatives to task-specific models because they handle diverse downstream tasks, including anomaly detection and forecasting, without per-series training. However, time-series data undergo distribution shifts, and the dissimilarity between two regimes is commonly scored with statistical measures such as Wasserstein-1, where a higher score is read as a more severe shift. In systematic experiments using three established severity measures on nine regime shifts from three standard traffic datasets, we show that these measures do not reliably predict degradation for instance-normalized TSFMs. The regimes rated most severe are not the regimes that degrade the models most, and degradation reaches 29% in the lowest-scoring regime. In most cases, the audit shows no positive relationship between measured severity and model degradation. We provide an equivariance-based stress-testing analysis that explains why severity readings can become decoupled from model degradation.

title: Reading or Remembering? Measuring Temporal Contamination in Language Models
summary: Language models are now used to read central-bank text for economic forecasting, but most were trained on text written after the documents they read. A model reading a 2021 FOMC statement may already know that inflation rose in 2022, so part of its apparent skill can be memory of the outcome, a temporal form of test-set contamination. We measure this memory on FOMC statements and minutes from 2000 to 2026 by comparing modern open models with chronologically consistent models, which are trained only on text from before a fixed date. Asked about past GDP outcomes given only a date, models that cannot know the answer still reach an AUC of up to 0.64 from priors on dates and eras, so chance is the wrong baseline. Against these memory-free models on the same questions, most modern models recall which years had strong growth. Membership-inference scores sort documents by era and document type rather than by whether a model saw them, as exact counts in an open pretraining corpus show. In real-time nowcasts, every lookahead premium we estimate on US GDP is smaller than the forecast comparison can detect at macroeconomic sample sizes, and none on GDP or inflation survives correction for multiple testing. Lookahead audits should therefore measure memory directly against memory-free models on the same items.

title: Benchmarking memory and nonlinear processing capacity of quantum recurrent neural networks for time series prediction
summary: Quantum machine learning has emerged as a promising approach to time series prediction. While quantum reservoir computing has been widely explored for this setting, variational quantum models tailored to sequential data remain comparatively understudied, largely because they are difficult to train. In this work, we present a rigorous benchmark of variational quantum recurrent neural networks (QRNNs) on time series prediction tasks, focusing on two key capabilities: memory and nonlinear processing. We introduce a task-driven methodology that quantifies model capacity, enabling an intuitive and fair comparison across architectures, including classical recurrent baselines. We evaluate the proposed framework on two generic benchmark tasks and on a synthetic dataset describing a chaotic system. Overall, the quantum models achieve performance comparable to their classical counterparts, but classical models scale better with the memory size within the range studied. Notably, one QRNN variant shows higher average capacity on the task designed to jointly probe memory and nonlinear capacity. Moreover, our results show that quantum models offer better capacity when we are able to find a good parameter initialization. However, the increasing sensitivity to initialization leads to a lower probability of finding good solutions as the model size increases. These results provide a principled starting point for designing richer quantum recurrent architectures and for assessing where they may offer practical benefits.

title: ONAM: Fitting Orthogonal Neural Additive Models for Post-Hoc Interpretability of Black-Box Predictions
summary: Modern machine learning models, such as artificial neural networks, achieve high predictive performance through increasingly complex black-box architectures, limiting their use in settings where transparency, interpretability, and fairness are required. Here we present the R package ONAM, which provides a novel and practical implementation of functional decomposition, a technique to facilitate the interpretability of black-box models through structured effect representations. ONAM implements an algorithmic framework for the post-hoc decomposition of predictions into components associated with different input features. The package is designed for usability and efficiency, including functionalities for visualization as well as quantitative measures to assess interpretability. As a model-agnostic method, it can be applied to a wide range of prediction models. We describe the mathematical foundations, algorithmic design, and software architecture of ONAM. A central result of the proposed methodology is that the resulting decomposition satisfies the condition of hierarchical orthogonality, thereby guaranteeing that all components are identifiable and uniquely defined.

title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
summary:
Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting.
  In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

title: SciResearch-Eval: Evaluating Scientific Judgment in Autonomous Experimental Agents
summary: We introduce SciResearch-Eval, an interactive benchmark of scientific judgment built on a standard laboratory problem: measuring a material's thermal properties by heating it and fitting a heat-conduction simulator. An agent designs its own experiments, uses a supplied simulator that may be under-resolved or physically wrong, and reports each property with a 95% interval. To our knowledge it is the first benchmark to combine agent-designed experiments, a deliberately flawed simulator, and proper scoring of calibrated intervals against exact ground truth. On a held-out split (93 tasks, 9 models, 2,511 episodes), models handle procedural traps. When the simulator is missing physics, most report wrong values while stating they are 95% sure: their ranges contain the truth in 20-62% of cases, against 94% for GPT-6 Astra and 99% for Claude Fable 5.2. At default effort the failing Claude 5.5 models rarely diagnose the missing physics (Opus in 35% of episodes, against 66% for Astra), and even when they do, their ranges often miss; Astra and Fable design experiments in which the flawed simulator is accurate, such as gentle heating, which keeps Astra calibrated even when it does not name the cause. Asking for wider intervals does not help; stating the strategy improves interval scores 1.6-2.5-fold, replicated on a pre-registered fresh split, but coverage barely moves. A pre-registered effort ablation shows that the correction is latent in the Claude 5.5 models: at maximum effort Opus improves more than tenfold and is no longer detectably behind Astra at default, but only with 13-31 times more reasoning; older and open-weight models gain nothing. Fable 5.2 is the most accurate model at default effort (interval score 1.9 times better than Astra's) but writes 6 times as many tokens, and at Astra's token count it falls short. We release the environment, graders and harness.

title: Seen but Unsaid: Locating and Repairing Cross-Image Comparison in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often fail to match a point or an object across two images, even when the answer can be decoded from their own hidden states. We trace this failure from the visual tokens to the answer letter, in Qwen3-VL (2B-32B), InternVL3.5-8B, and Gemma-3-12B, on synthetic shape matching, same-instance point correspondence (HPatches), and semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), and find two distinct failure points, a small set of attention heads that carries the comparison, and a repair that touches 0.02% of the parameters. Two failure points: exact copies are compared but not read out. An answer-position probe exceeds the calibrated output by 15 to 25 points in every family, for nameable and unnameable shapes alike, and steering along the probe's direction moves no more answers than random directions. Semantic correspondences are present in the visual tokens but never reach the answer. One pathway: redistributing the cross-image attention of 16-32 heads, with its mass preserved, removes 17-22 points of synthetic and 15-32 points of HPatches accuracy, against at most 7 for random or attention-matched heads. A lever that training finds on its own: training only these heads' query and key projections raises SPair-71k accuracy by 28.3 points (Qwen3-VL-8B) and 25.1 points (InternVL3.5-8B), beats both layer-matched and attention-matched heads, and transfers to HPatches and BLINK. An unconstrained all-layer adapter routes 21-51% of its gain through the attention of the same heads, against at most 7% for random heads, and does so by changing what they read (83-86% of the effect) rather than their weights. Every decision rule was frozen before its run, and every reported number is recomputed by independent verification scripts.

title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

title: Procedure without Judgment: What Small Language Models Learn under an Exact Verifier
summary: When an authorization policy blocks an agent's tool call, the audit log should name the facts that forced the decision and nothing more. For an executable policy over an enumerable context space this minimal sufficient reason can be computed exactly, so an explanation is scored against ground truth rather than a proxy for it. We use that exactness to ask what a model can learn from a verifier that has no error in it. The explainer sees one request and one decision, never the policy, and has thirty turns in which it may call the policy on altered requests and ask whether a candidate set of facts is sufficient. Frontier models find the exact reason about half the time with the tools alone, and one sentence telling them to shrink the answer lifts Haiku 4.5 from 58% to 75%. A 4B model fine-tuned on 2000 traces of the deletion algorithm reaches 92% on the policy it was trained on. Teacher kind is what moves this: at matched data size the algorithm-taught student leads the frontier-taught one in all three training seeds, and the two arms never overlap. What the student learns is a fixed schedule of sufficiency checks, and the schedule does not travel. On three public policies it never saw, its answers stay sufficient (94%) and stop being minimal (48%), while Haiku under the same sentence is exact on all 47 episodes. Reinforcement learning from the exact reward leaves held-out accuracy where it was and inverts the strategy, from probing the policy to spending the entire budget on sufficiency checks. The oracle made the effect of training legible, but it did not make training better.

title: Algorithm Distillation for Safe In-Context Reinforcement Learning
summary: Safe in-context reinforcement learning (Safe ICRL) asks a policy with fixed parameters to improve on an unseen constrained task from its interaction history while aiming to keep its cost within a budget. Prior work studied Safe ICRL on five benchmarks in three families: a grid world with a hidden goal and obstacles (DarkRoom), continuous navigation where goals and hazards stay invisible until reached (PointGoal, CarGoal), and locomotion with a hidden velocity limit (HalfCheetah, Ant). Safe Algorithm Distillation (Safe AD), trained on the learning histories of a safe RL algorithm, has shown adaptation failures in prior evaluations. For example, in the locomotion tasks its return stays below zero, and it rarely reaches the goal in CarGoal. We revisit two parts of Safe AD. First, we distill a budget-aware teacher with two phases. It searches for the hidden task, exploring more when more budget remains. After its first reward or cost, an expert policy exploits the task within the remaining budget. We collect the teacher's histories under fixed or dynamic budgets. Dynamic budgets increase the occupancy entropy of the return and budget inputs in every environment, and at test time they improve return and lower cost in DarkRoom and HalfCheetah. Second, we propose A-Lag, a test-time adjustment that reweights the distilled policy's actions by their predicted cost, with an adaptive Lagrange multiplier that is updated from the costs observed. In our experiments, A-Lag had lower mean episode cost than Safe AD in all five environments, with lower mean final return in four.

title: Tensorized Automata: Algebraically Informed Representation Learning for Sequential Decision Making
summary: Task representations for sequential decision making should describe both an objective and progress toward it. We present an algebraically informed pipeline that uses the relational structure and language semantics of alternating finite automata (AFAs) to learn control features and compile compact execution operators. AND-OR message passing learns task and state vectors; selected configurations define an event-driven Boolean matrix operator. We prove that initial and successor language coverage make its carrier represent the exact residual after every prefix, with a sufficient capacity bound in terms of reachable configurations. Conjunction and disjunction use the same pipeline. Fidelity and composition audits evaluate copied formulas and learned disjunct assignments. In five-policy-seed XLand experiments with larger training pools, pooled execution-state vectors outperform raw carrier bits and task-blind conditioning across three task pools under two rejection rewards. They achieve 77.3\% success on multi-event tasks and 99.4\% on a four-task stratum with 33--128-state minimal DFAs, using 16 operator slots. LetterWorld results show useful residual conditioning alongside a remaining gap to RAD. These results connect algebraically informed representation learning to compact task execution and useful policy conditioning.

title: Almost Controlled: The FDR of Benjamini-Hochberg on Weighted Conformal p-Values
summary: Weighted conformal p-values generalize conformal inference to cases with covariate shift. One way to use them is to pass them to the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure, either to decide which test units to select or to detect outliers. But weighted conformal p-values may not be positively dependent, so we want to know: does BH still control the false discovery rate (FDR) in finite samples? Based on experiments, it appears to, but we prove it doesn't. We give two counterexamples, certified in exact rational arithmetic, where the FDR exceeds its target level $q$. We also identify how large the difference between the FDR and $q$ can be. With $n$ calibration points, $m$ test units and weight ratio $B$, the relative excess $\mathrm{FDR}/q-1$ is bounded by a function of $n$, $m$, $B$ and $q$ that is of order $\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ when $Bm/(nq)$ is small. The bound holds for every configuration with $B\le n$ and every $n$. This order can be reached when multiple non-null test units share a common threshold: in a Poisson-limit model, that configuration's excess is $c(q)\sqrt{Bm/(nq)}$ to first order as $B/n\to0$ and then $m\to\infty$. For some fixed distributions with this structure, the excess decreases only like $n^{-1/2}$ as $n$ grows. If every test unit is null, the excess is $O(B/n)$ at fixed $m$, and in certain configurations it grows linearly with $m$. To assist practitioners in judging how large the FDR can be, we turn that bound, which depends only on $n$, $m$, $q$ and $B$, into a lowered BH level with proved finite-sample control, and give a much less conservative rule of thumb that covers every worst case we were able to find but provides no guarantee.

title: Leverage-Enhanced Sampling Owen Method for Explainable Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recently, the Shapley value has been widely applied in machine learning for feature importance analysis and model explainability. The multilinear extension of games proposed by Owen (1972) expresses the Shapley value as the integral of partial derivatives along the main diagonal of the cube. Direct evaluation of this integral requires exponential-time computation of the partial derivatives. To improve computational efficiency, we propose a sampling-based estimation strategy within Owen's multilinear extension framework, combining stratified sampling with coalition leverage scores. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly reduces computational costs while maintaining explanation accuracy.

title: Learning from Duality in Neural Network Field Theories
summary: We develop neural realizations of positive-level Wess-Zumino-Witten models using bosonic Wakimoto and fermionic Fourier-Berezin fields. Level-rank duality connects the charged sectors of the fermionic construction, where explicit neural observables recover conformal block data and enable the transfer of information about unknown correlators between paired theories. We also show that distinct neural presentations of the same continuum current algebra exhibit different finite-width behavior, with approximation accuracy depending on architecture, regulator, and parameter distribution. These results connect the exact mathematical structure of conformal field theory with the expressive and computational properties of neural field theories.

title: Differentiable Exact Learning
summary: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.

title: Network Intrusion Detection Adaptability under Spurious Labels: A Noise-Aware Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning Framework
summary: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) must incrementally adapt to emerging attacks, even when only a limited amount of labeled network traffic is available. Consequently, Few-Shot Class-Incremental Learning (FSCIL)-based NIDSs have gained growing attention. However, existing FSCIL-based NIDSs are highly vulnerable to label noise in newly-observed attack classes. To address this limitation, we propose NAFN, a noise-aware FSCIL-based NIDS framework that reduces the impact of mislabeled data during incremental adaptation. NAFN consists of two components: (i) Noise Detection, which identifies and removes mislabeled biflows using noise-detection algorithms, and (ii) Feature Sampling, which estimates class-conditional embeddings from clean biflows, calibrates them with base-class statistics, and resamples synthetic features to recover the original biflow count. The framework follows the Rethink Few-Shot (RFS) teacher-student paradigm with lightweight nearest-neighbor or logistic regression classifiers, and various pretraining & memory selection strategies. Experiments on CSE-CIC-IDS2018, Edge-IIoT, and IoT-NID datasets show that NAFN effectively preserves prior knowledge and maintains strong incremental performance even under 50% label noise, consistently improving new-class F1-scores over non-denoised baselines, up to +52%, while being time-efficient and robust in cross-network and high-noise incremental settings. The implementation is publicly available to foster reproducibility.

title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
summary: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

title: Generative Data Augmentation Without External Data: An Empirical and Theoretical Study on Deep Networks
summary: Generative data augmentation adds samples from generative models to a classifier's training set. Many influential studies use generators pre-trained on large external datasets, and so mix the value of synthetic data with knowledge transferred through pretraining. We study the case without external data, where each generator learns only from the classifier's own training set, and ask when and why adding generated samples to that training set raises or lowers the classifier's test accuracy. We train classifiers with four backbones on six datasets, two of them medical, adding samples from four generators. We bound the excess risk of a classifier trained with synthetic data, that is, how far its population risk can lie above the minimum risk within its hypothesis class. The bound charges synthetic data for the total variation distance between the real and generated distributions and credits synthetic data for a larger training set. The gain from adding synthetic data, the fall in population risk, is at most the excess risk of the real-only classifier, which trains on the real images alone. Read through the bound, the experiments suggest that synthetic data help most when our classifiers detect only a small discrepancy between the generated and real data and the real-only classifier has room to improve, and that synthetic data help little or hurt when the detected discrepancy is large. Generators with a larger lower bound on the total variation distance, a bound that we estimate from our own classifiers, tend to help less on five of the six datasets, and on the CIFAR datasets the most accurate backbone gains the least. The bound gives these directions but not the size of the largest gains, most of which traditional augmentation also reaches at the same number of optimizer steps.

title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

title: A Scalable Multi Task Learning Framework for Modeling Demographic Disagreements in Annotation Tasks
summary: Annotators from different demographic backgrounds often disagree in systematic ways due to varying lived experiences, cultural contexts, and their relationship to the content. When such disagreement occurs, one group's perspective may sometimes warrant prioritization because they hold an epistemically advantaged standpoint or bear greater stake in the outcome. For example, when assessing toxicity of posts on social media, it may be important to prioritize a targeted group's viewpoint. We propose a Stakeholder-Aware Joint Multi-Task Learning (SAJ-MTL) framework to jointly model demographic disagreement both across- and within- annotator groups. The model uses conditional gradient routing to handle sparsity induced by group-conditional labeling, and parameterization supports customized weighting of groups in different task settings. SAJ-MTL improves group-level performance in toxicity detection through better context-aware understanding of demographic-sensitive content. Only annotator group-membership information is required, which is more practical than existing methods requiring more privacy-invasive individual-level annotator details. Our scalable architecture is also computationally efficient to support large-scale deployment.

title: Comments on "Deep Fréchet Regression"
summary: We discuss the Journal of the American Statistical Association (JASA) discussion paper "Deep Fréchet Regression" and explore an alternative perspective based on conditional flow matching. We propose learning covariate-dependent transport directly within the response space, avoiding separate manifold learning and reverse mapping. This perspective offers a potentially more flexible framework for incorporating geometric structure and modeling full conditional distributions.

title: A Reinforcement Learning Method to Navigate SMEFT Operator Space
summary: In particle physics, discrepancies between experimental measurements and Standard Model (SM) predictions are commonly interpreted within new theoretical models. In this context, the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) provides a general framework encompassing a broad class of models. However, exploring the enormous space of possible SMEFT operators rapidly becomes a challenging combinatorial problem: many operators can contribute simultaneously to different observables, their effects are correlated, and distinct operator combinations can provide comparably good descriptions of the data. In this work, we formulate the exploration of the SMEFT operator space as a sequential decision-making problem using reinforcement learning (RL). Our RL agent employs a lightweight actor-critic architecture with approximately 40K trainable parameters in total. Rather than searching for a single best-fit theory, our method is designed to discover a diverse set of high-quality theory hypotheses. We test the method in a complex phenomenological environment comprising 132 observables across several sectors of particle physics, including 24 measurements that deviate from their SM predictions by more than $1.5σ$. We show that the learned RL policy efficiently constructs multi-operator theories that substantially improve the global fit. Comparisons with independent random-subset and random-sequential searches demonstrate the ability of the RL policy to navigate this large combinatorial space. Our results establish RL as a systematic framework for exploring diverse patterns of new physics (NP) interactions within SMEFT.

title: Variational Monte Carlo for Quantum Excited States via Nested Low-Rank Approximation
summary: The electronic Schrödinger equation encodes a molecule's electronic structure and quantum properties, but solving it scales exponentially with the number of electrons. Solving this equation with neural-network variational Monte Carlo (VMC) has reached chemical accuracy on the ground state of small molecules; extending this success to excited states is constrained by two existing paradigms. Penalty-based methods need $K$ Laplacians per step but require tuning the overlap-penalty weights against the energy gaps they aim to compute. Natural excited states VMC (NES-VMC) is penalty-free, but it combines the $K$ ansatzes into one determinant, whose local energy requires $K^2$ Laplacians per step. We resolve this trade-off via low-rank approximation (LoRA) reparameterization of the rank-$K$ variational objective. The reparameterized objective admits a VMC-compatible stochastic gradient estimator via MCMC sampling from the per-state Born densities, and a sequential nesting scheme recovers the lowest $K$ eigenstates in eigenvalue order. The resulting algorithm, NestedLoRA-VMC, inherits a global optimality guarantee from the LoRA principle. On the first-row atoms Li through Ne at $K=10$, its accuracy is comparable to that of NES-VMC and of a state-of-the-art penalty-based method.

title: Just sort it! A note on the LP behind rank-one anti-loop edits
summary: Weight-space programming removes the thinking loops of a small reasoning model by a rank-one edit W' = W + u v^T of an MLP output matrix, where u is a loop direction and v is the solution of a sparse Linear Program (LP) over the neuron activations. We investigate whether the LP is needed. We replace it by a sort: we take the 8 neurons whose activation has the smallest coefficient of variation, and give them equal shares of the push that the LP solution realizes. On Qwen3.5-0.8B the sorted edit scores 67.0% on 1000 problems (MATH-500 and GSM8K) against 67.4% for the LP edit and 9.5% for the unedited model; the paired difference is -0.4 points, with 95% confidence interval [-2.9, +2.1], inside a non-inferiority margin of 5 points declared before the runs. On three further sampling seeds the difference is -0.6 points, interval [-2.0, +0.8], and -0.8 points, interval [-2.3, +0.6], when the dose is set without the LP. The sort does not solve the LP, but the neurons it shares with the LP solution carry most of its mean push. The outcome is that, on this model, the edit acts as a nearly constant bias along u.

title: Emergent Steering Beyond Endpoint Alignment in Chemical Reaction Models
summary: Machine learning models for chemical reaction prediction are usually evaluated by endpoint accuracy, but endpoint correctness alone does not reveal how a model represents chemical transformation or why it fails. We introduce UniRxnAxis, a unified forward-retrosynthesis framework that models both tasks as direction-conditioned endpoint redistribution in a shared latent space. By aligning source states, transformed states, and encoded target endpoints, UniRxnAxis enables directional auditing of learned latent updates. This shared latent geometry allows the learned displacement (from the encoder source state $S_0$ to the decoder-facing transformed state $S_1$) to be decomposed into an endpoint-parallel component and an endpoint-orthogonal residual, which we call emergent steering. Our evaluation shows that emergent steering is functionally important: in retrosynthesis, it recovers most of the model's utility, remains effective under random, shuffled, and prototype controls, and directly affects which bond edits are promoted or suppressed. The residual-over-parallel ordering persists across alignment strengths, after decoder-interface calibration, against angle-matched random axes, and in a second graph-edit architecture, although its magnitude depends on the reference axis and optimization. The decomposition also supports a proxy taxonomy of model-side failures, showing how reaction models can be audited beyond endpoint accuracy.

title: Do Embedding-Map Distances Guide LLM Ideation? Four Tests Against What Came Next
summary: A popular ideation recipe treats an embedding map of existing work as a guide: pick points far from everything and decode them into ideas. I test four ways such distances could guide ideation against what appeared later. (1) Far random directions are not text: no later item reaches a raw cosine above about 0.10 with one (after centring or whitening, 22 of 24 cells stay out of reach), and an LLM decoder shown a target's neighbours, with score-only feedback, writes those neighbours in all six target sets. A neighbour-free search writes coherent text at median cosine 0.57 and 0.47 to interior gaps, beating the nearest existing item on 15 and 14 of 20, but only 0.07 and 0.06 to far points. (2) On k-means cells of a past-only map, the registered hole score mostly tracks cell size and position; three density-based gap scores forecast which cells grow fastest at or below chance (AUC 0.30 to 0.66) and add nothing to momentum in Steam and arXiv, with patents inconclusive; more isolated new Steam games are slightly better reviewed. (3) LLM continuations of arXiv papers stay closer to the source than papers that cite it, under three user prompts and against proposal rewrites (gpt-4o) and April-December 2023 papers (OLMo). Critique lengthens this step beyond content-free revision, replicated on 150 new papers. Revealing a real follow-up's title turns the ideas by 0.032 along a follow-up-specific direction beyond revision; reviewer, oracle and distance feedback add 0.13, 0.08 and 0.34 of that turn (upper bounds 0.46, 0.46, 0.70), and their turn is not separable from revision or their longer step. (4) For inspiration material graded by distance, no inverted U was detected, on an anticipation margin that tracks format more than content. Original tests were registered before running, follow-ups (thirteen requested in two AI-agent reviews) after the main results; all are dated only by local git commits.

title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
summary: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

title: MegNIST, A Benchmark for Non-Invasive Inner Speech Decoding
summary: MegNIST is a benchmark dataset for developing and evaluating machine learning methods for inner speech decoding from magnetoencephalography (MEG). The dataset comprises 12,000 trials of a single participant imagining speaking the digits zero through nine, recorded across four sessions. Each trial contains 306-channel MEG recordings sampled at 250 Hz, preprocessed using signal space separation, filtering, and downsampling. Data are provided as pre-defined training (10,000 trials), validation (1,000 trials), and test (1,000 trials) splits, with entire experimental runs assigned to each split to preserve temporal independence. The dataset is available in both BIDS format for neuroimaging analysis and as serialised tensors for machine learning workflows. Baseline classification results demonstrate that imagined digits can be decoded significantly above chance. Standardised splits, validated baselines, example code, and a PyTorch-compatible loader in the pnpl Python library enable straightforward integration with machine learning frameworks, lowering barriers for researchers to rapidly develop and benchmark inner speech decoding methods for non-invasive brain-computer interfaces.

title: Self-attention is a Dyson equation for many-body machine learning
summary: Why does symmetric sum-pooling (DeepSets) predict ground-state potentials to sub-meV accuracy, yet fail for correlated wavefunctions and excited states? Sum-pooling is a mean-field (Hartree) model: its $O(1/N)$ off-diagonal Jacobian suffices for nearsighted ground-state energies, but erases nonlocal two-body correlations. We show that self-attention is a real-space Dyson iteration whose Boltzmann (softmax) kernel acts as a two-body self-energy. Because physical Hamiltonians act pairwise, Löwdin's 2-RDM theorem and the Galitskii--Migdal relation guarantee that iterating a two-body propagator captures the full energetics of correlated matter. When fitting a fractal backflow determinant, DeepSets blurs the nodal surface onto a mean-field envelope, whereas self-attention recovers the fractal attractor. Seen through this lens, the unreasonable effectiveness of attention is not an accident; in a universe built from pairwise interactions, two-body attention is all you need.

title: Train After You Measure: a Pre-Registered Learning Curve for Fine-Tuning Typed Decision Models on One User's Labels
summary: Fine-tuning a small typed decision model on one user's email labels did not clear the margin we pre-registered over a logistic regression trained on the same labels. In earlier work, about two hundred labels and a TF-IDF logistic regression had the highest point accuracy on this inbox, though not significantly above the best hosted model; we ask whether the same labels, given to a decision model, close the gap. A first registered study, on a generic 4B base with cross-validation and message type only, stayed below the baseline at every label budget (-1.8 to -7.3 points). The main study was registered before any fine-tuning run: a fixed test set of 135 emails never used for selection, LoRA adapters on the public Tev1-0.8B and Tev1-4B decision models, nested subsets of 50 to 587 labels, two seeds and five decision fields on a free T4 GPU. Four of its five hypotheses are refuted--two in the fine-tunes' favour--and one is confirmed for one model. On message type the 4B model misses the registered three-point margin at 400 labels (+2.6) and passes it with all 587 (+3.3); with all labels both models are above the baseline by +0.7 and +3.3 points, where one email is 0.74 points and a 95% interval is about 15 points wide, and the 4B model is clearly ahead in type macro-F1 (0.581 vs. 0.406). On the three action switches the baseline is ahead at every label budget for both models (0.931 vs. 0.904 and 0.899 mean accuracy with all labels), at under a millisecond per question against 306 and 1681 ms. The 0.8B type curve barely improves after 300 labels and then falls. The baseline never predicts the two rarest classes (7 offers and 8 spam in the training pool); the fine-tuned models find spam in some runs, not consistently across seeds. We list the explanations we did not test and say when a new attempt would be worth making. Scripts are public; weights and emails are not.

title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
summary: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

title: Learning What Pairs Miss for Higher-Order Multimodal Alignment
summary: Contrastive learning beyond two modalities now scores the whole tuple with multilinear products, volumes, and fusion heads, critics that can represent the joint distribution. In practice these critics still behave like bags of pairs. Their negatives break at least two of the three pairs, a single pairwise check rejects them, and when most samples can be solved by pairs the higher-order term receives almost no gradient. To solve this problem, we propose CHORD (Contrastive Higher-Order Residuals with Decoys), which trains a residual against decoys drawn from a calibrated pairwise model, negatives that the pairwise model finds plausible, so that rejecting them often needs all three modalities. Drawing decoys costs one inner-product query over a memory bank, and the optimal residual is the log-ratio between the data and the pairwise model, so the decoy loss also bounds what that model misses. On M3-Mix, where one in ten training samples needs all three modalities, our CHORD improves accuracy on those samples by 21.2 percentage points over the strongest of eight baselines. CHORD also gives the best two-to-one results on every real dataset, and its residual improves other retrievers without retraining.

title: Federated TD Learning in Heterogeneous Environments with Average Rewards: A Two-timescale Approach with Polyak-Ruppert Averaging
summary: Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) provides a promising way to speedup training in reinforcement learning when one has access to multiple edge devices that can operate in parallel. Recently, it has been shown that even when these edge devices have access to different dynamic models---such as cars or robots with differing system configurations---an optimal convergence rate that has a linear speedup proportional to the number of devices is achievable. However, this result requires that the algorithm's stepsize be chosen in a manner that depends on the unknown model parameters. Also, it applies only to a discounted setting, which has been argued to fit episodic tasks better than continuing control tasks. In this paper, we obtain finite-time bounds for heterogeneous FRL with average rewards. We show that optimal convergence rate and linear speedup are achievable even with a universal stepsize choice, independent of the underlying dynamics. To achieve our result, we modify the existing one-timescale FRL method to a novel two-timescale variant that additionally incorporates iterate averaging. We remark that this idea also extends to other settings already studied in the literature, such as the homogeneous FRL or the heterogeneous case with a discounted cost function.

title: Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion for Decomposable Generative Models
summary: Generative model pre-training typically optimizes a model as a whole without explicitly organizing its parameters for selective reuse. Decomposable pre-training instead learns reusable components for downstream adaptation while retaining strong generative performance. However, existing knowledge diversion methods incur substantial parameter overhead through weight factorization and rely on fixed component assignments to induce specialization, potentially compromising in-distribution generation quality. We therefore propose Specificity-Guided Knowledge Diversion (SGKDiv), which learns how generative knowledge is shared and specialized for effective generation and selective downstream reuse. SGKDiv constructs Knowledge Units from paired feed-forward channels, preserving native computational structure without SVD-based reparameterization. Calibrated condition-wise routing combines a shared usage prior with conditional adjustments, while complementary regularization shapes their allocation, diversity, and magnitude. Together, these designs replace predefined component assignments with adaptively learned and explicitly regulated knowledge specialization. Experiments across diverse model and training settings demonstrate better in-distribution generation than dense and MoE baselines, alongside stronger downstream adaptation than representative PEFT methods across eight datasets.

title: Representational Change Under Self-Consuming Training: A Sparse Autoencoder Analysis
summary: Large language models are increasingly exposed to model-generated text, raising the possibility that future models will be trained recursively on the outputs of their predecessors. Prior work on such self-consuming training loops has largely focused on output quality and downstream performance, leaving their effects on internal representations poorly understood. We study how representations evolve across five generations of self-consumption and whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) remain reliable under this shift. At each generation, we compare a lineage trained on synthetic data with a matched control trained on real data under the same training settings. We evaluate how well SAEs trained before self-consumption transfer to later generations, measuring reconstruction and sparsity across SAE widths, architectures, and model layers. We then fine-tune the original SAE on each generation and use sparse probing to test whether task-relevant information remains concentrated in a small number of latents or becomes more distributed across the representation. We find that zero-shot SAE performance degrades progressively under self-consumption, with growing reconstruction and sparsity gaps that vary substantially across layers. Fine-tuning largely restores reconstruction, but not feature-level usefulness: task-relevant information remains accessible in the full latent space while becoming less concentrated in individual features. These results show that self-consumption induces representational drift and that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to establish that an adapted SAE remains equally useful for interpretation.

title: TEMPO: Regime-Aware Operator Learning with Locally Adapted POD Bases
summary:
Operator learning approximates the solution map of a parametric partial differential equation from data, enabling fast prediction at new parameter values without repeated simulation. The dominant approach fits a single global low-rank basis, typically a proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), to all solution snapshots. This fails when the snapshots span qualitatively different solution shapes, from smooth diffusive profiles to near-discontinuous shocks.
  We propose TEMPO (Trajectory Expectation-Maximization Mixture of POD Operators), a two-phase framework for regime-aware operator learning. In the offline phase, TEMPO recovers latent regimes via expectation-maximization, fitting a dedicated linear or nonlinear basis to each discovered regime. In the online phase, a gating network and per-regime branch networks are trained jointly, routing new inputs to the regimes at inference.
  We test TEMPO on Burgers' flow, Sod shock tubes, Coanda flow, Darcy flow, Navier-Stokes flow and the heterogeneous Helmholtz equation. With 64 total POD modes, TEMPO gives 18.61% test error on Burgers', compared with 19.61% for global POD. It also gives lower errors on Coanda and Helmholtz.

title: Video recordings and play behaviour annotations of group-housed dairy calves on two Dutch farms
summary: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.

title: Anchoring Motion, Refining Trajectories: Generalizable Continuous Neural Decoding
summary: Brain activity encodes motor information across multiple temporal scales, enabling continuous neural control beyond discrete action recognition. However, existing methods are typically tailored to specific subjects and tasks, with direct neural-to-kinematic mappings that can entangle subject-specific neural variability with task-dependent motion patterns, limiting generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce AMRT, a shared neural decoding framework for heterogeneous electrode configurations and movement paradigms. Motivated by cortical encoding of movement direction and speed, AMRT adopts a two-stage design that anchors local motion through velocity estimation and refines the resulting trajectories over longer horizons, encouraging reuse of local motion tendencies across subjects and tasks. Across three datasets, AMRT generalizes to unseen trials and subjects and demonstrates transfer potential across neural recordings and movement paradigms, highlighting the potential of shared neural representations and anchor-and-refine decoding for generalizable continuous neural control.

title: Wavelet-Energy-Driven Dynamic Patching for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Patch-based transformers tokenise a time series into fixed-size, uniform windows, which commits the model to a single temporal resolution even though real signals are multi-scale. The discrete wavelet transform (DWT) is a natural alternative because it decomposes a signal across scales. A growing body of work makes the wavelet filter learnable, on the assumption that a more flexible wavelet forecasts better. That assumption has rarely been tested in isolation, because a single reported improvement usually credits three things at once. These are the use of any multi-resolution decomposition, the choice of wavelet and training the filter. We introduce a forecaster that turns a learnable-DWT per-scale energy map into variable-length patches by merging adjacent windows that share a dominant scale. Three findings follow. First, most of the improvement is there before any filter is learned. A frozen wavelet beats a fixed-patch baseline on eight of the nine datasets by 1.5% to 7.8%, and on four of them it recovers all of the gain. Traffic is the one exception, where it is 1.2% worse. Second, learning the filter gives a further improvement on only some datasets. It helps on three of the nine datasets and makes Traffic 2.7% worse. Third, having variable-length patches helps, but exactly where their boundaries fall does not. A fixed-size uniform grid, even with its patch size tuned per task, is worse than our variable-length patches on 27 of 36 settings. Recomputing the boundaries from the learned filter at every step, rather than caching them once, never helps. The improvement in wavelet-based forecasting comes from the multi-resolution structure and the variable-length patches it induces, not from making the wavelet learnable. In practice, start from any valid wavelet, cache the patch boundaries once and treat training the filter as a per-dataset decision rather than a default.

title: Disambiguating Moral Circuits and Moral Features in Language Models: Moral content, normative judgment or cue words? Evidence from 14 models
summary: Interpretability methods can locate the attention heads and sparse autoencoder (SAE) features that change the answer a language model gives to a moral prompt, e.g., whether "Stealing medicine for a dying child is morally" continues with "justified" or "wrong". Such a component could respond to moral content, to the judgment of conduct by any norm, or to the word "morally" in the prompt. We built 227 minimal pairs of short phrases, validated by five annotators, whose two versions differ in a moral standard, in another kind of norm (prudence, etiquette, aesthetics or evidence) or in a descriptive quality, and showed them to 14 open-weight models (Llama, Gemma and Qwen, 1B to 14B, base and instruction-tuned), with and without the word "morally". In every model, the heads that change the moral answer belong to an evaluation circuit the models use for every kind of normative judgment we tested: these heads carry the same share of the effect for moral as for other normative pairs (pooled ratio 1.00, 97.5% confidence interval [0.92, 1.07], with the word; 0.90, [0.84, 0.96], without it), and the models need them as much for both. The models need these heads also when nothing in the prompt asks for a judgment, and on 400 scenarios of the ETHICS benchmark, where removing them takes away 37 to 39% of the difference between acceptable and unacceptable scenarios, against 1 to 3% for ten random heads. The SAE features we located respond mostly to the word "morally" rather than to what the phrase is about. The models represent the category of a pair (the standard the annotators assigned to it): it can be read from their hidden states, and, in the eight models we tested, removing the direction that carries it weakens the moral verdict by a few percent, and more than the other verdicts in seven of them. We release the pairs, the ratings, the code, the trained SAE dictionaries and the result files.

title: Can AI Mature a Model's Geometry? Training-Free Weight Baking in LLMs
summary: Can an AI make a trained language model more mature, in the sense of a better organized latent space, by looking only at the geometry of that space? An analyst model reads a fixed-size digest of topological descriptors of the layers of a frozen target and proposes a transformation, which closed-form ridge regression writes into the feed-forward weights without gradient training. Using lightweight models, 126 runs show that category purity rose on unseen words and sentences, benchmark accuracy stayed within sampling error, and the analyst matched a category-aware heuristic with gentler edits. In a five-model round robin approach, 16 pairs raised purity and four left the target unchanged. The results provide a baseline for future work on LLM-guided, training-free model editing without using raw weights.

title: Programmable Semantic Interventions: Learning Causal Carriers from Behavioral Programs
summary: Causal abstraction explains a frozen network by aligning its activations with the variables of a simpler, interpretable model, and checking that interventions on the two agree. Finding such an alignment currently requires a counterfactual dataset: for every pair of prompts, the answer the network ought to give once the variable has been changed. In practice, those labels are produced by an executable algorithm for the behavior, written before studying the model supposed to implement it. However, the criterion these methods optimize only leverages the answer an intervention should produce. Here, we develop an approach that lets the investigator define that relationship directly: the answers the variable can produce, and which of them an intervention should yield. We call this interface a semantic program and introduce Programmable Semantic Interventions (PSI): a low-rank activation subspace learned so that interchanging it changes the model's answer as the program declares, with the expected answers read from the frozen model itself. On the MIB benchmark PSI performs on par with supervised alignment at matched data and training budget, without curated pairs, and it needs no ground-truth labels; while on natural science questions with gold labels withheld, it tracks the model's own answers better than a subspace trained on gold labels. The declaration also fixes a coordinate system with known semantics, enabling donor-free steering: jointly training PSI for both localization and control realizes 94.8% of held-out requests for answers the investigator chooses, without the need for donor prompts.

title: High-probability Uniform Mixing via Dobrushin Contraction and Accelerated Hamiltonian Monte Carlo
summary: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, since its invention and subsequent rise to widespread use, has been motivated by its ability to accelerate convergence to equilibrium compared to diffusive methods, both in terms of dependence on condition number and dimension. In the present work, we establish this acceleration simultaneously in both aspects for critically damped Metropolis-adjusted kinetic Langevin with persistent uniforms. More precisely, for target measures $μ(dx)\propto e^{-U(x)}dx$ with $m$-strongly convex, $L$-gradient Lipschitz, and $L_H$-Frobenius Hessian Lipschitz potentials, we show that the method mixes to $\varepsilon$-accuracy in total variation using $\mathcal O\bigl((κ^{1/2}+L_H^{1/2}m^{-3/4})\,d^{1/4}\bigr)$ gradient evaluations up to logarithmic factors, both uniformly over starting points in domains of high equilibrium probability and from warm starts. The proof incorporates ideas from previous studies by Bou-Rabee and Chen et al. that show either aspect of acceleration separately, into novel coupling technology. This new coupling technology for general Markov chains extends earlier frameworks aimed at capturing fast local equilibration in the presence of slow global mixing. Specifically, via a weak-$(1,1)$ maximal inequality that follows from Hopf's maximal ergodic theorem, we uncover a stability mechanism in high-probability domains with respect to equilibrium. This enables straightforward localization to naturally arising domains of fast local mixing, and seamlessly fits broad local frameworks via Dobrushin contraction, Wasserstein contraction and local Harris' theorems. We develop the Dobrushin formulation.

title: Deep Learning for Physicists: From Linear Regression to Reasoning Models
summary:
These lecture notes are based on an introductory course on neural networks and deep learning that the author taught in the School of Mathematical Sciences at Queen Mary University of London in 2023/24 and 2024/25. The author, however, is a physicist, and it shows: wherever possible, ideas are explained with physical intuition rather than heavy formalism. Readers with a background in physics or mathematics who want a self-contained, introductory route into modern machine learning may therefore find these notes particularly friendly.
  The notes start from maximum likelihood, least squares, linear regression and (stochastic) gradient descent. They then cover neural networks, backpropagation, the vanishing gradient problem, batch and layer normalization, overfitting and regularization, adversarial examples, and the kernel method. The second half turns to natural language processing: word embeddings, recurrent networks and LSTMs, the attention mechanism and Transformers, and large language models, including scaling laws, the history of GPT, instruction tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, hallucination, alignment faking, chain-of-thought reasoning and test-time scaling. The emphasis on large language models reflects requests from the students.
  The notes are aimed at third- and fourth-year students in the UK system. Because the course was also taken by students from other departments, very little is assumed: even basic material such as matrix multiplication is explained from scratch, so readers familiar with it can safely skip such parts. No originality is claimed; the aim is a coherent, intuitive path through the material.
