On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.

title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
summary: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
summary: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
summary: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

title: Chain-of-Thought Hidden States Reveal Task-Solving Directions for Direct Answers
summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. We start by labelling each CoT hidden state as recovering if patching it into the direct prompt yields the correct answer, and failed otherwise. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. We then show that the representation space of the direct prompt holds a direction for each question that leads the model, in a short generation, to the correct answer more often than CoT does. Specifically, we rotate the direct prompt's last hidden state once, before generation, towards a direction built for each question from its own recovering and failed states. Across 25 tasks, these directions raise the direct prompt's mean accuracy from $46\%$ to $85\%$ on LLaMA 3.1 8B (CoT: $69\%$) and from $52\%$ to $86\%$ on Qwen 2.5 7B (CoT: $77\%$), with a tenth of CoT's tokens. CoT is thus not the shortest route to this accuracy, and these directions can be used in future work to train models to align their states with them.

title: Think Offline, Act in Real Time: Self-Improving Visual Game Agents through Code
summary: Pre-trained models can read screens and reason about games, yet on an unfamiliar game, an agent still has to learn to play. We ask how an agent can self-improve on such a game from a few of its own attempts, in real-time visual games where the agent sees only the screen and the game keeps running while the agent thinks. We study two kinds of policy that can carry this improvement. In model as policy, a model selects actions during play; we adapt real-time chunking so that committed actions keep executing while the model reasons, and train a 2B controller for this interface. In code as policy, a model writes, tests, and revises a program between attempts, and the program acts during play. Across 170 GameWorld tasks, with at most eight one-minute executions per run, code as policy reaches 47.80% mean progress, against 30.90% for our trained controller, and leads in all five game categories. Improving the controller's weights on a single game, by contrast, yields only modest gains. These results favor letting a model think offline and storing what it learns in a program that acts in real time. Project repository: https://github.com/TabibitoQZP/SIGame

title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.

title: AGAMOTTO: An AI-Enabled Framework for Time-Critical Tactical Course-of-Action Evaluation and Generation
summary: Current command and control (C2) platforms lack integrated simulation capabilities that would allow commanders to dynamically explore courses of action (COAs) during live operations. This paper presents ongoing research and contributions to the development of AGAMOTTO (Advanced Guidance and Analytics for Military Operations, Tactical Threats, and Outcomes) as part of the overarching NGC2 program, which advances the Army's efforts to modernize C2 systems, such as the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK). The paper outlines the current design, preliminary findings, and the remaining research tasks, with an emphasis on how the completed work will support tactical decision-making in future time-constrained environments. While the full system is still under development, initial development and results demonstrate the feasibility of AGAMOTTO. Early experiments highlight both the potential benefits and practical constraints of deploying AI-enabled tools in operational settings, and introduce lessons learned and a viable training strategy to make AI-generated COAs feasible in tactical scenarios.

title: NaviGATE: Noise-Aware Dual-View Generation for Multimodal Knowledge Graph Reasoning
summary: Multimodal knowledge graph reasoning (MKGR) aims to infer missing facts by jointly exploiting relational structures, textual descriptions, and visual evidence. Existing embedding-based methods effectively capture graph topology, but their fixed multimodal representations are less effective for query-specific fine-grained semantic reasoning, while generation-based methods are vulnerable to noisy retrieval and may produce invalid entities. To address these challenges, we propose NaviGATE, a noise-aware generative framework for MKGR. NaviGATE first aligns graph-derived structural representations with textual semantics, then performs structure-aware internal knowledge activation by fine-tuning the multimodal language model with multimodal entity summaries and injected structural tokens. In the noise-aware dual-view instruction tuning stage, NaviGATE jointly optimizes retrieval-free and retrieval-aware views: reliable retrieved candidates are reinforced through contrastive logit sharpening, while misleading candidates are suppressed through parametric consistency distillation. In inference, structure-constrained decoding restricts generation to valid entities in the target knowledge graph. Experiments on standard benchmarks show that NaviGATE consistently outperforms strong unimodal, multimodal, and generation-based baselines, and remains robust under noisy retrieval scenarios.

title: Do Frontier Model Ingredients Add Up? A Replicated Factorial Study of Small Language Models
summary: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. These findings apply to our small-model training setting; the expert models also have greater total capacity. The practical lesson is to test promising components together and repeat the comparisons before deciding which ones to keep.

title: MECI: Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction for Multimodal Entity Linking
summary: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. However, existing methods often suffer from element dominance due to their reliance on coupled interactions or coarse global aggregations. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. First, to capture multi-element mention-entity correspondences, we develop a Multi-view Experts Network that leverages a "divide-and-conquer" strategy for decoupled feature learning to mitigate element dominance, supported by a KL-guided routing mechanism that governs expert specialization and collaboration. Furthermore, to model cross-modal complementary correlations, we propose a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Module, where a dynamic modality-aware weighting network refines interactions across hierarchical semantic levels, thereby integrating multi-granular evidence to counteract element dominance. Finally, we incorporate a generative semantic refinement stage that utilizes large language models for zero-shot re-ranking. Extensive experiments on WikiDiverse, RichpediaMEL, and WikiMEL show that MECI consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving Hits@1 by 1.95%, 7.30%, and 2.31%, respectively.

title: ABSClaw: From Invented Worlds to Reality-Grounded Social Simulation
summary: LLM-based artificial societies exhibit rich behavior but often lack scientific grounding: personas and environments are assumed, interaction networks are synthetic, and simulators are generated as free-form code, making results difficult to tie to real populations and sensitive to the backbone model. We argue that simulated worlds should be sampled from observed data, while simulation logic should be implemented by composing operations from a shared, task-independent vocabulary. In this paper, we introduce ABSClaw, a zero-code agent that compiles natural-language requests into executable, reality-grounded social simulations. ABSClaw grounds who acts, where they act, and with whom they interact in survey and census data, geospatial sources, and real networks. It expresses state transitions through 26 atomic operations. To support an open and extensible ecosystem, ABSClaw further allows capabilities to be added as lifecycle-scoped skills without modifying its core. Furthermore, we propose ABSBench, a benchmark of 193 real-world social-simulation tasks. On ABSBench, ABSClaw achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated social simulators. Three real-world case studies show that grounding personas, environments, and interaction networks each improves agreement with observed outcomes. With one runtime skill, ABSClaw executes 13 population-scale simulations, collectively involving 25 million agents. Together, these results demonstrate ABSClaw's real-world fidelity, extensibility, and scalability.

title: The Largest Tractable Subclass of Multi-Scale Allen Temporal Reasoning
summary: In this paper, we propose a novel model for temporal reasoning over multi-scale intervals. We show that this model yields a complete reasoning framework and exhibits other particularly interesting properties. Furthermore, we identify the maximal tractable subalgebra for this model, as well as for the other complete model, in the qualitative scales context, which exhibits weaker properties but whose results can be derived by transfer from our new model.

title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
summary:
GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time.
  We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine.
  Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

title: Probing agent overeagerness in realistic settings with continuation audits
summary: Frontier coding agents increasingly exhibit overeagerness, taking surprising, sometimes reckless actions beyond a user's mandate --- reported in recent system cards from frontier model developers. These cases are surfaced through internal deployment monitoring, which requires private traffic and is out of reach for open-weight models and independent evaluators. Automated alignment audits are the natural alternative, but capable models increasingly recognise the synthetic setup and adjust their behaviour. We introduce Continuation Audits, a pipeline that grounds the auditor on a prefix drawn from a real coding-agent transcript and directs it to continue the trajectory toward a seeded behaviour. Because the prefix is drawn from a real session, the auditor only needs to maintain a realistic setting rather than manufacturing it. We validate the method on SWE-Chat prefixes: on a paired subset of 90 audits a judge cannot reliably distinguish continuations from their source sessions (realism win rate 0.42 vs.\ 0.43), and across all 900 audits verbalized eval-awareness does not exceed the rate observed in the unaudited real sessions. Applying the pipeline to three recent models across three seeds, we find each model leads a different seed --- DeepSeek~V4~Pro on colleague-credentials misuse, GPT-5.6~Terra on file-permission bypasses, and Kimi~K3 on treating diagnostic questions as instructions. Kimi~K3 additionally continues to bypass file-permission protections after an explicit CLAUDE.md prohibition while the other two stop entirely, corroborating Moonshot's own report of excessive proactiveness.

title: Mitigating fix reversal: Counterfactual constraints for function-level vulnerability detection
summary: Function-level vulnerability detectors often exhibit fix reversal, assigning a higher vulnerability probability to a fixed version than to its vulnerable counterpart. Fixes usually lengthen functions, and larger length increases are associated with more severe reversal. Code-transformation experiments indicate that fix reversal mainly stems from a length shortcut: vulnerability probability increases with function length when content is fixed. We propose CFVul to address this problem. Sliding-window encoding covers complete functions, retaining fix information beyond the truncation boundary. During training, a content constraint encourages the vulnerable version to receive a higher vulnerability probability under a common length input. During inference, a length constraint averages vulnerability probabilities over fixed reference lengths, reducing the influence of actual length changes. On PrimeVul, CFVul achieves a fix-pair ranking metric, PairRank, of 59.4\%, exceeding the existing methods compared. For fixes that increase function length by more than 15\%, PairRank rises from CodeBERT's 25.8\% to 48.4\%. PairRank also improves in experiments with four additional models and three additional datasets. By weakening the length shortcut, CFVul reduces cases in which fixed versions receive higher vulnerability probabilities than vulnerable versions. It requires only existing fix pairs and applies to multiple pretrained code models, facilitating adoption in existing detectors.

title: Study and Improvement of Search Algorithms in Stochastic Perfect-Information
summary: In this article, we generalize Unbounded Minimax, the state- of-the-art search algorithm for deterministic zero-sum two- player games with perfect information to the framework of stochastic zero-sum two-player games with perfect informa- tion. We experimentally show that this generalized algorithm achieves better performance than the main stochastic search algorithms.

title: What the model knows but does not say: monitoring medical LLMs through verbalized thoughts
summary: Efforts to keep clinical language models safe have concentrated on what enters and leaves the model, but a manipulated model can return an answer that looks entirely ordinary. Here we show that the model's own internal state, rendered in plain language, exposes manipulations the output conceals. Using a natural-language autoencoder, we translate the activations of a multimodal LLM (Gemma-3-27B) into text and let an input-blind judge read this verbalized internal state (the thoughts channel) and the model's answer separately. Across two clinical attack objectives (omitting a pathology, covertly recommending a drug), two input modalities, and two delivery mechanisms, the thoughts channel caught the injection significantly more often than the answer in all eight injected conditions (p<0.05), while both channels held near-zero false-positive rates on clean inputs; the omission result carried over to Llama-3.3-70B. The thoughts channel also registered unsafe clinical requests as harmful while the model was still reading them, before it decided whether to refuse. None of this requires retraining: an off-the-shelf verbalizer and a general-purpose judge are enough.

title: Nothing to Declare: Steering a single neuron increases concealment in AI teams
summary: Recent research suggests that individual neurons can have interpretable roles in AI behaviour. In Qwen3.5-4B, steering along one neuron's output direction increased decisions to conceal information more in teams than alone across five scenarios, even when teammates provided no messages. When all members participated and received steering, collective concealment increased in four scenarios, while inter-agent messaging helped temper concealment under steering. Moreover, removing the neuron's contribution had negligible effects. Collective settings can therefore change how an internal intervention affects AI behaviour.

title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern $I \ldots V \rightarrow I$. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.

title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
summary: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

title: Let a Small Model Read First: Faster Prefill for Long Interleaved Image-Text Inputs
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.

title: Keeping Shielded Data-Driven Controllers Safe Under System Evolution via Model Consistency
summary: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) increasingly contain data-driven controllers, which raise safety concerns given their black-box nature. A common mitigation is to enforce system safety via a shield around the controller, which restricts the inputs based on assumptions about the physical system. However, these assumptions are usually fixed and may become invalid as the system evolves (during development or due to component degradation), possibly leading to unsafe behavior. We address this limitation in a model-driven approach that treats both the data-driven controller and safety shield as first-class models that are integrated into a virtual single underlying model (V-SUM) alongside system models. We describe system evolution as changes in the associated models, such that consistency checking yields a continuous assessment of safety guarantees. In case of inconsistencies, consistency-preservation rules automatically update the models and restore a valid safety shield. We evaluate our approach on a reach-avoid task for a unicycle system. The results show that consistency-driven evolution effectively maintains safety guarantees under system changes and provides a principled basis for evaluating and restoring performance.

title: Resolution as Attention for Efficient Agent Memory Perception
summary: LLM-based agents accumulate extensive interaction histories when solving complex, long-horizon tasks, making efficient memory management critical to their performance and scalability. While existing memory management methods primarily focus on what to retain or retrieve, they often overlook how much perceptual detail should be allocated to individual past interactions. We posit that effective agent memory depends not only on the information preserved, but also on the granularity at which each past interaction is perceived. Motivated by this insight, we propose Resolution as Attention (RAA), a memory perception mechanism that uses visual resolution as a means of attention allocation across interaction histories. RAA renders past interactions as images and dynamically adjusts their resolution at every step according to their relevance to the agent's upcoming decision, preserving fine-grained information for critical interactions while reducing visual-token consumption for less relevant ones. To adaptively determine the perceptual fidelity of each interaction, we train a lightweight relevance estimator with teacher-model guidance and further optimize it to preserve the agent's decision consistency at a reduced visual-token cost. Experiments across multiple tasks and backbones show that RAA reduces token consumption by over 50% without compromising task performance. Moreover, RAA can be integrated as a plug-in perception layer with existing memory management methods, yielding further token savings and revealing adaptive perception as a complementary dimension of agent memory.

title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
summary: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.

title: Risk-Triggered Search: Behavior-Preserving Safe Control
summary: Pre-trained visual world models generate multi-step action plans from current and goal observations, yet terminal-proximity objectives fail to prevent forbidden-zone traversal or rigid-body collision sliding. Purely visual interfaces may lack analytical dynamics, structured states, or explicit collision geometry, requiring internal prediction of action-conditioned process risk. We propose Risk-Triggered Search (RTS) for frozen Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) world models. Rather than relying on static state features that cannot distinguish candidate plans sharing an observation, RTS unrolls action-conditioned future latent prefixes in the frozen world model and trains a lightweight risk head with process-violation supervision. To intervene selectively while preserving safe nominal behavior, RTS uses the same predicted prefix-risk criterion as both the search trigger gate and hard feasibility gate: safe nominal plans execute directly, whereas alarms trigger local Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) search to minimize nominal deviation within the feasible set. To prevent isotropic Euclidean minimal modification from shrinking obstacle-directed actions into zero-amplitude stalling, we introduce an amplitude-preserving metric $d_{\mathrm{AP}}$ that retains tangential progression while maintaining a unique zero at the nominal plan. Under unified gating and this unique-zero condition, bypassing safe-state search yields closed-loop trajectories strictly identical to every-step same-kernel search. Evaluated under a process-safety benchmark and Safe Arrival Rate (SAR) metric across five tasks, RTS improves SAR over Direct by 12.67--41.67 percentage points on navigation and articulated control and +2.08/+4.17 pp on Cube/PushT boundary cohorts, maintaining 100% action identity with every-step search while cutting controller time by 17.71%--70.41% across 1,968 paired trajectories.

title: CaDO: Formal Verification-Guided Multi-Agent Framework for Causal Dataset Repair and Generation
summary: High-quality causal reasoning datasets are essential for developing models with reliable causal understanding, particularly in specialized domains. However, existing datasets frequently suffer from incorrect annotations and structural imbalances, which can lead to biased predictions and limited generalization. To address this issue, we propose CaDO (Causal-Engine-Guided Multi-Agent Data Optimization), a multi-agent framework for automated diagnosis and repair of causal reasoning datasets. Our framework consists of three key stages: formal causal reasoning, multi-level diagnosis, and automated data repair and generation. First, a Formalizer Agent translates natural language questions into formal causal queries to minimize semantic deviations and make retrieval and verification more explicit and tractable. Second, a dual-level diagnosis mechanism employs independent Critic Agents to identify sample-level errors while analyzing query-type coverage and label distributions to detect dataset-level structural imbalances. Finally, the framework employs reusable repair operators grounded in formal causal semantics to correct erroneous samples, while Explorer and Expander Agent collaboratively produce diverse and semantically consistent new samples. Experimental results show that CaDO significantly outperforms the strongest of five data cleaning baselines in 16 out of 18 experimental settings, improving downstream model accuracy by up to 9.1%. Moreover, at least 95% of the samples flagged by CaDO are defective, and on CLadder, CaDO incorrectly modifies 92.2% fewer correct labels than an LLM-based judge, demonstrating its effectiveness and reliability. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/thisissyu/cado.

title: Temporal Rank in Recurrent Neural Networks
summary: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a natural framework for temporal modelling, yet are often dismissed due to their sequential, non-parallelisable computation and difficulty in capturing long-range dependencies, typically attributed to vanishing and exploding gradients. We identify a distinct and under-explored limitation: an information bottleneck induced by rank-constrained hidden state dynamics, which limits the number of independent input directions that can be preserved over time, as reflected in the rank of the input-to-state mapping. We show that this constraint restricts temporal capacity independently of gradient stability. To address this, we introduce structured high-dimensional state dynamics that preserve temporal separability and prevent saturation of the input-to-state Jacobian over time. On controlled sequence tasks, the resulting model exhibits rapid learning despite remaining strictly within a standard RNN formulation. Our results demonstrate that RNN performance is governed by the evolution and preservation of temporal rank, and suggest that mitigating gradient pathologies alone is insufficient without explicitly maintaining temporal capacity.

title: Enhancing Active Learning Performance with Initial Data Selection Based on Foundation Models
summary: In active object detection, selecting the initial labeled pool is essential, especially in complex datasets with expensive labeling and low resource budget. This study presents an active learning framework designed to optimize the initial training cycle of active learning for the object detection task. Our approach diverges from traditional methods by utilizing feature-based clustering from the YOLO-World model and refining images based on objectness scores rather than relying on uncertainty sampling in the initial cycle. This approach focuses on finding samples with various features and emphasizes training in areas where the foundation model is most confident. Doing so helps the model better understand different types of objects. For subsequent cycles, we employ a consistency-based sampling technique to maintain the robustness of the training process. To evaluate our method, we use two complex datasets called Aquarium and NWPU VHR-10, which are well known for their diverse object sizes and challenging conditions. In the NWPU dataset, our method increases mAP50 by an average of 6.6% in image-based evaluation. Moreover, the image refinement method shows an improvement of approximately 11% in object-based evaluation. The results show improvements in model performance and labeling time, demonstrating the advantages of using foundation models in early cycles of active learning. An implementation of the algorithm is available at https://github.com/Mhrshd-fllh/ALBoost-FM

title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
summary: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.

title: LLM-Assisted Multi-Fidelity Bayesian Optimization: Fusing Expert Knowledge with Numerical Data
summary: Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) reduces engineering design cost by combining inexpensive low-fidelity (LF) models with a few accurate high-fidelity (HF) evaluations and sequentially selecting designs to evaluate. However, when HF data are scarce, the LF-HF discrepancy is difficult to learn from numerical data alone, especially when physics omitted in the LF model makes it design-dependent. Yet even without sufficient data, domain experts often know which physics the LF model omits and under which conditions its effect grows. Existing multi-fidelity (MF) models cannot use such qualitative knowledge directly, but large language models (LLMs) can interpret it and compare designs accordingly. The proposed LLM-Assisted MFBO adds a knowledge basis to the conventional MF model: from an expert description of the omitted physics, an LLM judges which of two designs requires the larger signed residual correction, and a pairwise Gaussian process converts these judgments into the basis. HF data calibrate its contribution and sign, so the knowledge is not trusted blindly. On a lithium-ion battery design problem, the proposed method reduced the regret area under the curve of conventional MFBO by 61%. Knowledge quality, rather than the choice of LLM, determined whether the search was accelerated, as shown by a controlled study that varied the two independently. A knowledge-level ablation further quantified the contribution of each knowledge statement. These results show that LLM-interpreted expert knowledge can complement numerical data as an information source in MFBO.

title: PIPETTE: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce PIPETTE, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. PIPETTE employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that PIPETTE produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

title: Towards Pose-Robust Few-Shot Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Fine-tuning a vision-language-action (VLA) model on a few dozen demonstrations is the standard way to put a manipulation policy on a robot, yet the resulting policy silently assumes that the camera and the robot base stay exactly where they were during data collection: a bumped tripod or a base re-docked a few centimetres away makes it reach for the wrong place. We show that both failures are one phenomenon, a change of the camera-to-base extrinsic that the policy has memorised, and that the robot carries everything needed to undo it. We introduce WACO, a world-anchored canonicalization framework for VLA models: the arm, placed by forward kinematics at the measured joint angles, serves as a metric calibration target, and the static scene serves as the world anchor that tells a moved camera from a moved robot. From a single RGB-D frame, WACO estimates both shifts without ground-truth extrinsics or extra data, canonicalises the image to the calibration viewpoint and the state, action and start pose to the calibration base frame, and fine-tunes the unmodified policy under the artefacts of its own estimator. We also introduce LIBERO-PoseShift, the first benchmark for RGB VLAs with graded camera, base and compound shifts. Across LIBERO-PoseShift, the LIBERO-Plus camera track and four real-world tasks on a UR5e robot, WACO consistently outperforms the standard few-shot recipe and prior viewpoint-robust methods, raising shifted success by 13.2 points in simulation and by 36.7 points on the real robot, recovering 90% of the simulation gap to a ground-truth oracle and 87% of the real-robot gap, and establishing a new state of the art among methods that use no perturbed training data, with no test-time calibration. Project page: https://peacelwh.github.io/WACO/.

title: Semantic Context Handoff with On-Demand Evidence for Long-Horizon Agents
summary:
Traditional long-horizon LLM agents often hand off context through full-history prompting, retaining all previous action--observation interactions. As execution proceeds, this history keeps growing, increasing inference cost and potentially degrading accuracy. Existing methods control this growth by preserving compact conclusions while removing earlier observations, but doing so can discard evidence that later becomes relevant. We introduce Semantic Context Handoff (SCH), whose central abstraction is state--evidence separation: a compact semantic state carries the agent's current interpretation, while supporting action--observation evidence remains separately addressable and can re-enter context when later execution makes it relevant, without separate summarization or retrieval-model calls.
  Empirically, SCH improves long-horizon agent performance while substantially reducing context cost. In a controlled 150-task SWE-bench study, SCH's evidence recovery improves Pass@1 from $80.0\%$ to $86.9\%$ at essentially unchanged token use and execution time. In the complete-system comparison, SCH achieves 86.9% Pass@1 while using 43% fewer tokens and 41% less wall-clock time than the strongest baseline by task performance. Across models and benchmarks, SCH consistently reduces token use relative to full-history prompting while remaining competitive with or improving upon the evaluated baselines. Trajectory analysis confirms that SCH recovers evidence from substantially earlier parts of the interaction history rather than merely preserving a recent context window.

title: When Figures Disagree with Text: Evaluating Autonomous Visual Evidence Verification in Scientific Papers
summary: Scientific figures carry evidence for the claims that cite them, so reviewing a paper means checking that a figure agrees with the text, and not only describing what the figure shows. Benchmarks of figure-text verification typically hand the model the figure, the claim, or the knowledge that an inconsistency exists, which leaves untested whether a model can find the figure worth checking in a complete paper, relate a visual element to the claim it conflicts with, and recognize the conflict. We study this autonomous setting on 31 full manuscripts, each carrying a reviewer-documented figure-text inconsistency from PRISMM-Bench that is hidden from the model. Six multimodal models review each PDF under a neutral prompt, and we then add one input at a time to the same manuscripts. Of 1,445 open-ended reviews, 60.6% mention the flawed figure, yet a grading rubric accepts only 3.3% as diagnosing its contradiction; a blind audit finds the rubric lenient, so we read these as rubric-accepted rates and compare conditions rather than absolute values. In a separate controlled run, naming the figure, without stating that it is flawed, raises rubric-accepted diagnosis from 4.3% to 20.4%, while a consistency instruction and coarse visual cues do not. When the contradiction is visible only in the rendered figure, text-only review yields no accepted diagnosis, while review of the rendered pages with the figure named reaches 15.8%. A baseline that lets the model choose which figures to check, ranked by centrality, stays at 4.8%. Deciding what to verify is thus a large part of the difficulty, and the selection rule we tested does not resolve it. Multimodal document understanding should be evaluated on whether a model can propose what to verify, not only answer questions about a figure it is handed.

title: OCTR2A: Real-Time RGB-to-BEV Trajectory Projection and Forecasting at Urban Intersections
summary: Trajectory forecasting at urban intersections is often studied assuming that reliable bird's-eye-view (BEV) motion histories are available, which in practice requires costly resources such as LiDAR, aerial views, HD maps, or calibrated infrastructure. We address this upstream perception-to-forecasting problem by reconstructing and predicting agents' BEV trajectories only from paired opposite-corner RGB cameras mounted on existing urban infrastructure at variable heights at inference time. We introduce the Opposite-Corner Trajectory Reconstruction and Anticipation Architecture (OCTR2A), a modular pipeline integrating per-view detection with class refinement, geometric cross-camera matching, transformer-based BEV projection, and egocentric GRU forecasting, trained in cascade and mainly supervised with a soft multi-scale spatial-overlap loss. Since no public benchmark provides this sensing configuration, we introduce R3ST++, a Blender-based synthetic benchmark built from SIND trajectories that provides synchronized opposite-corner views, cross-view correspondences, and BEV ground truth, while also serving as a deployment-support simulator for site-specific fine-tuning. Experiments on these datasets show that, with 12 observed and 12 predicted frames at 10\,Hz, OCTR2A achieves projection~-~forecasting ADE/FDE of 0.144/0.140~-~0.154/0.241~meters in real time on a single consumer GPU. Evaluated on ground-truth BEV histories, the forecasting module improves over the strongest state-of-the-art methods on SIND by 66.7\%/41.7\% ADE/FDE. Transfer experiments on TUMTraf-V2X show that R3ST++ pretraining supports adaptation to real-world roadside domains with different sensing configurations.

title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
summary: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.

title: Can Weight-Space Programming Alter Learned Ethical Priorities?
summary: We investigate whether a weight edit can alter how a model trades off honoring a commitment against benefiting more people. In a concept-supervised text model, we alter fitted choice weights so that the benefit required to override a formal pledge is larger than for an ordinary promise. Across six independently trained text readers, the edit selects the larger group in both orders on 100% of targeted ordinary conflicts and 83.3% of targeted formal conflicts. It preserves the source model's success rates on smaller conflicts and its factual accuracy. The remaining formal-conflict failures coincide with errors reading a beneficiary number. A separate classifier demonstrates why this distinction matters: reusing a factual answer passes an unconditional choice test but fails to preserve small-gap promises. In a YOLO11n pilot on COCO128, a bias edit increased small-target matches from 3/43 to 9/43, and an equivalent score calibration reproduced the retained detections. These exploratory results show a way to test selective changes to learned priorities in a model with an exposed trade-off mechanism. Whether the method can discover such changes in less structured language models remains open.

title: Reducing Inference Cost of Coding Agents with Timeout Cascades
summary:
AI coding agents have become one of the most popular applications of large language models. Yet, agentic AI comes at the cost of a tremendous amount of GPU compute resources, which limits its profitability and its viability at scale. In this paper, we investigate whether smaller, cheaper models can cut this cost without sacrificing accuracy.
  We evaluate 36 popular large and small open-weight models released since 2024 on a software engineering benchmark, and find that recent small models are closing the accuracy gap compared to their large counterparts. We investigate the structure of this gap and find that the gap is highly concentrated around hard tasks that small language models fail to solve while achieving remarkably good accuracy for easy and medium complexity tasks. Following this observation, we show that by utilizing a hybrid inference strategy that tries a small model first and escalates to a large one only when needed, we can achieve up to 33% reduction in total GPU-hour costs and 16.4% on all tasks from SWE-bench Verified, without sacrificing accuracy. Strikingly, this simple cascade nearly matches an oracle-style task router, highlighting a practical path for deploying cost-aware coding agents in production without complex learned task routers and with minimal engineering complexity.

title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
summary: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

title: Fuse to Recognize the Unseen: Class-Relative Infrared-Visible Fusion for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
summary: Visible-infrared image fusion leverages complementary thermal cues to enhance visual perception, particularly under challenging illumination. However, such perceptual complementarity does not readily translate into semantic gains in open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS), where CLIP-based models are predominantly pretrained on RGB imagery. Directly introducing IR information may instead disrupt RGB-language alignment, turning promising thermal cues into semantic interference that undermines unseen-class recognition. Our pixel-level RGB-IR semantic analysis reveals that class-relevant thermal cues can correct certain RGB misclassifications while preserving reliable RGB predictions, motivating RGB-anchored, class-relative thermal cue selection. Based on this insight, we propose EmergeFuse, an infrared-visible fusion framework for OVSS that selectively converts complementary thermal evidence into unseen-class semantic corrections. Specifically, class-relative cue selection evaluates RGB-IR semantic responses and calibrated thermal evidence relative to RGB predictions, generating class-relative correction requests through competitive selection. Text-contrast image rectification then translates these selected requests into semantic rectification directions through text contrasts, guiding evidence-gated feature updates to realize complementary thermal evidence for unseen-class recognition. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate gains of up to 4.755% in unseen-class mIoU and 15.730% in strict complementary conversion rate over existing fusion methods, while maintaining competitive fusion quality.

title: AutoPI: Taxonomy-Guided Adaptive Red Teaming for Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
summary: Prompt injection is the dominant unsolved security risk for LLM agents, and the community now agrees that robustness must be measured against adaptive attackers rather than fixed benchmark injections. Many adaptive red teamers exist, and most are built to maximize attack success rate (ASR). Yet ASR counts how often a target breaks, not in how many different ways. A red teamer can achieve a high ASR by reusing a few techniques that work, leaving the others untested and absent from the attacks used to harden models. We present AutoPI, an adaptive red teamer designed to find many different ways to break a target, not just to break it often. AutoPI uses PIAtlas, a taxonomy of prompt-injection techniques, both to guide its search and to measure coverage. For each scenario, an attacker LLM writes an injection for every sub-technique in the taxonomy and then reworks the ones that fail using feedback from an LLM judge. The method is black-box and training-free, it plugs into existing benchmarks in place of their fixed attack templates, and it stays up to date as the taxonomy evolves. We evaluate AutoPI on AgentDojo and IPI Arena against open-weight and proprietary target models. Alongside ASR, we report technique coverage, the fraction of taxonomy classes, techniques, and sub-techniques that yield at least one successful injection. On AgentDojo, AutoPI finds a successful injection against Qwen3.6-35B in all six classes of the taxonomy and for more than 90% of its techniques. Against Claude Haiku 5.5, the most robust target we evaluate, it achieves between 20% and 50% higher ASR and between 25% and 400% higher class-level coverage than recent state-of-the-art adaptive red teamers, while requiring no training. We release our code and the generated attacks to support reproducible, coverage-aware evaluation.

title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

title: Beyond Corpus-Driven Imitation: Evolving Musical Mindsets in the Agentic Orchestra via Quantum Reinforcement Learning
summary: This paper presents a framework for computer-aided music composition and performance based on quantum reinforcement learning and multi-agent interaction. We introduce the agentic orchestra, where musical agents evolve distinct mindsets through trial-and-error engagement with a musical environment, rather than through training on large datasets. The agents are implemented as parameterised quantum circuits. They evolve distinct compositional behaviours, referred to as mindsets. This enables the exploration of musical decision spaces using quantum superposition and entanglement within a hybrid quantum-classical loop. We present two complementary agent architectures: atomistic agents, which process pitch and rhythm independently, and holistic agents, which handle pitch and duration as unified note events. Mindsets are shaped through musically grounded reward functions, which can be combined and weighted to develop different mindsets across agents. The resulting system positions quantum computing agents less as autonomous composers and more as adaptive musical partners, each developing its own musical personality through interaction rather than imitation. Demonstrations show how agents generalise their learned behaviour to previously unseen material, operating in interactive and offline batch modes using MIDI-encoded music. While quantum computers are still in development, experiments conducted on IBM quantum hardware confirmed that musically meaningful learning is achievable with existing quantum computers. For composers and performers, the agentic orchestra opens new possibilities for emergent, process-oriented musical creativity, offering a scalable foundation for quantum computer-aided music composition as quantum computing technology continues to advance.

title: FedE2E: One-Shot Federated Learning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving with Closed-Loop Evaluation
summary: Federated learning enables collaborative model training without sharing datasets. However, existing federated learning methods for autonomous driving typically require multi-round communication and lack closed-loop evaluation, while one-shot methods mainly focus on perception tasks. To address these limitations, we propose \method, a one-shot federated learning method for end-to-end autonomous driving. It comprises multi-client calibration, anchor-based feature alignment, and token-wise consensus distillation to distill knowledge from heterogeneous models. Closed-loop evaluation on Bench2Drive demonstrates the effectiveness of \method in both one-shot and multi-round federated learning. In the one-shot setting, it achieves a Driving Score of 55.85, which is 4.07 points higher than prior work. In the multi-round setting, it reaches 60.35 after five communication rounds, the best performance among all compared methods under the same number of communication rounds.

title: From Points to Trajectories: Rethinking Multimodal Alignment for Physical Events
summary: Advancing physical artificial intelligence (Physical AI) requires moving beyond static object recognition to ground how real-world mechanics (e.g., impact, friction, and force transfer) unfold over time. While multimodal aligners seek to capture these interactions by matching multi-sensor streams, prevailing architectures compress each temporal sequence into a single pooled embedding. We show that this paradigm fails on twin events: distinct physical executions recorded under identical task conditions. Collapsing the temporal dimension averages out transient cross-modal dynamics, effectively reducing physical event alignment to static scene recognition. Formally, we prove that as sequence length increases, any temporally pooled representation converges to the stationary recording condition. Consequently, as windows grow, no choice of loss function or embedding geometry can disambiguate twin events from pooled features alone. Instead, we show that physical events are uniquely identified by the event gap, namely the instantaneous, synchronous co-fluctuations across modalities that are erased by pooling and accumulate only along unpooled trajectories. To recover this signal, we introduce CounterPoint, a lightweight plug-in module that strips out each modality's temporal mean to score frame-level cross-modal agreement. Integrated across four state-of-the-art (SOTA) multimodal aligners, CounterPoint shifts representations from coarse condition matching to fine-grained physical event alignment, consistently outperforming existing temporal alignment methods.

title: What Survives the Shift from Text to Pixels? Conditional Protection against Prompt Injection in Image-Rendered Documents
summary: Multimodal language models increasingly answer questions over external documents, exposing them to indirect prompt injection: commands planted in untrusted content to hijack the response. Rendering untrusted content as page images lowers attack success on average, leaving open which injected operations survive rendering, at what utility cost, and whether failed image attacks reflect unread commands or commands read but not followed. We pair text and page-image versions of 191 English question-answering sources across six models, measuring marker appending, answer formatting, and answer replacement alongside clean Question-Answering utility. Rendering reduces append and format execution for every model, yet Qwen3-VL-8B still executes image-borne replacement at 77.96\%. Protection also depends on target type, rendering settings, wording, and repetition, and a search over eight fixed attack candidates largely closes the image deficit in appending and formatting for Qwen and Gemini, though not for GPT-5-nano. Utility ratios on original questions range from 93.31\% to 101.61\%, but Qwen falls to 61.99\% when answers combine two evidence spans. Illegibility cannot explain all failed attacks: models often transcribe and identify image-borne commands they do not execute, and trusted user authorization raises execution on unchanged pages. Inside Qwen, patching early attack-region states induces all three operations, more weakly in images. Attention blocking suggests why: a text command acts through its own positions, whereas visual encoding spreads an image command and its target across the instruction page. Rendering thus offers conditional protection, motivating evaluations that report security by model, operation, and attack budget alongside utility.

title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
summary: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
summary: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

title: Conditional What-If Generation for Radio Access Network Energy under Rare and Unseen Contexts
summary: Energy-saving mechanisms in RANs must balance energy reduction and network performance under varying traffic conditions. Conditional generative models support what-if analysis by generating plausible power-consumption trajectories for radio configurations and operating scenarios, helping operators evaluate energy-saving policies before deployment. However, representative measurements are costly and operationally constrained, so historical data cover only limited configurations and conditions, leaving some contexts poorly represented or unseen during training. In this paper, we study conditional generation of RAN power-consumption trajectories under decreasing training coverage, from well-represented to rare and unseen configurations. We first introduce a context-normalized conditional generator combining temporally aligned conditioning with configuration-dependent target normalization. It improves generation for well-represented configurations but becomes less reliable as training exposure decreases because target consumption is harder to estimate. We therefore introduce a prediction-based generative framework that decomposes power consumption into global prediction, residual level and scale correction, and temporal residual generation. Experiments on a commercial 5G RAN and a public dataset show that hardware metadata provides transferable information about residual scale, while limited target observations at inference improve generation through residual-level correction without retraining. An ablation study confirms that residual-level correction provides most of the gain. Both approaches outperform state-of-the-art methods for well-represented configurations, while the prediction-based approach also generalizes to rare and unseen contexts and, with one target observation, reduces median MAE by about 50% compared with TimeWeaver.

title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
summary: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

title: SpiderMark: Hybrid Watermarking for Generative AI via Algorithmic Injection and Learning-Based Verification
summary: The proliferation of diffusion-based generative models has intensified the need for reliable methods to trace and verify the provenance of AI-generated images. Existing watermarking approaches for diffusion models typically rely on isotropic frequency patterns and handcrafted detection metrics, which are prone to directional vulnerability and threshold instability across diverse image transformations. We propose SpiderMark, a hybrid watermarking framework that combines algorithmic frequency-domain injection with learning-based probabilistic verification, requiring no modifications to pretrained diffusion model weights. SpiderMark embeds a structured spider-web pattern, comprising radial spokes and concentric polygonal rings, into the Fourier representation of the initial latent noise, and trains a lightweight ResNet-18 verifier augmented with auxiliary similarity cues (PSNR and L1) to produce a continuous watermark confidence score for watermark detection. Across nine evaluation conditions, SpiderMark achieves the highest fixed-threshold Accuracy in eight, while retaining strong detection on unseen COCO prompts without verifier retraining. CLIP similarity and FID measurements show that these detection gains are accompanied by small measured differences in prompt alignment and distributional image quality. SpiderMark establishes that structured watermark geometry and learned probabilistic verification can be unified into a single, practical framework, bridging the gap between imperceptibility, robustness, and real-world verifiability for generative AI content attribution.

title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
summary: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.

title: VideoACE: Benchmarking Agentic Video Understanding through High-Frame-Rate Actions
summary: Agentic video understanding requires models to actively interact with video environments to gather evidence and form judgments. Evaluating this capability therefore requires assessing whether models can translate opportunities for interaction into better understanding. We introduce VideoACE, a benchmark for assessing video understanding under conditions that support sustained interaction. We focus on high-frame-rate action videos, where rapid, subtle changes make targeted observation especially valuable.
